Part 1: Before Monday (23 to 26 Oct)

Chapter 1 of 30

Your presentation for Monday: guide and script

When and how long: Friday evening: sections 1 and 2 (15 min), the script out loud with the slides, twice (30 min), and read and be ready to say your answers to Q7 (statistics at VTU), Q13 (paying for the pilot yourself), Q16 (how you counted the BrandMemory numbers) and Q20 (your own role in building Yuki) (10 min). Saturday: section 3, say Q1 to Q8 and Q17 out loud until they feel natural (1 hour). Sunday, after the mock: Q9 to Q16, Q18, Q19.

Your 7 slides

The same deck as the PDF you present from. Read the script below with these.

Meeting: Monday 26 October 2026, 14:00 to 14:30 Japan time = 10:30 to 11:00 India time, Google Meet. The link is in Dr. Ji's email of 22 Oct (thread "Fw: 【NAIST】Reception 2027M3055 ..."). Dr. Zhenlan Ji and Dr. Brittany Reid will interview you. Dr. Ji wrote: "you need to introduce yourself and your prospective research topic. Please feel free to prepare a short presentation (e.g., 5-7 slides)".

Files in this folder:

  • Sudhanshu_Pandit_SDlab_interview.pdf: present this one. It looks exactly as checked, on any computer.
  • Sudhanshu_Pandit_SDlab_interview.pptx: the editable deck, with the script in the speaker notes.

The deck was checked in two rounds. Round 1: five independent reviewers (a fact-checker against the papers, a visual designer, a "Dr. Reid" reader, a "Dr. Ji" reader and an interview coach), each followed by a skeptic who tried to disprove every finding. Round 2: a fresh fact, visual and interviewer check of the fixed deck and of the answers below. The claims on the slides were checked against your proposal and the paper PDFs.

1. How to present on Google Meet (practise this once before Monday)

  1. Before the call, open the PDF in Preview. Close other apps and turn on Do Not Disturb.
  2. Join the Meet at 10:25 IST. Camera on. Greet them first, without sharing.
  3. When they ask you to introduce yourself, say: "I prepared seven short slides, about five minutes. May I share my screen?"
  4. In Meet: Present now (the screen share button) → A window → choose the Preview window. Then in Preview press Cmd + Shift + F (View → Slideshow) and use the arrow keys.
  5. Keep the script on your phone or printed on paper beside the camera, not on the shared screen.
  6. After slide 7, stop sharing so they see your face for the questions.
  7. If sharing fails: say "Sorry, let me just tell you," and give the 2-minute pitch without slides. They can read the proposal they already have.

Alternative: upload the .pptx to Google Drive, open it with Google Slides, and use Present → Presenter view (it shows the notes in a separate window), then share that tab in Meet. Check the slides once in Google Slides first, because fonts can shift slightly.

2. The script (about 5 to 5.5 minutes)

Speak slowly. Look at the camera, not the slide. Do not read word for word: know the points, and use these sentences as your guide.

Slide 1. Title (about 30 seconds (65 words))

Thank you, Dr. Ji and Dr. Reid, for meeting me today. My name is Sudhanshu Pandit. My question is: which rules in a file like this CLAUDE.md do coding agents actually follow? For example, if it says put new tests in the tests folder, does the agent do it? And does keeping a rule change the quality of its code? First, a little about me.

Slide 2. About me (about 35 seconds (78 words))

I finished my B.E. in Computer Science and Engineering at VTU in May 2026, and worked in software engineering roles during my studies. Since November 2025 I have been an AI engineer on the founding team at Layerpath, where I build systems on top of large language models. I also build Yuki, a desktop AI agent for Mac and Windows. I use Claude Code and Codex every day and maintain their context files. My question comes from BrandMemory.

Slide 3. Where my question comes from (about 55 seconds (121 words))

BrandMemory takes a company's writing rules from its website and gives them to a model as context. When I measured the output, some rules had no effect. Some never reached the model, because they sat at the end of a long prompt that was cut off. Others lost to a default house style. I fixed both, then ran one A/B test on one product demo, without and with the rules. Contractions went from 6 to 0, and 'you' and 'your' from 15 to 1. That is one comparison, not a study. But it taught me to measure whether a model follows a rule, not assume it. Coding agents get rules the same way, so I want to ask this for them.

Slide 4. What is known, and the gap (about 60 seconds (129 words))

Your lab's papers show what developers write in these files, and Agent READMEs also found fewer indentation violations after an indentation rule was added, in two repositories. Gloaguen and colleagues found that a whole file does not generally raise task success and adds over 20 percent to cost on average; their traces suggest instructions are followed, but they do not test single rules. Zhang and colleagues removed 18 curated rules one at a time, but measured only task success. Huang and colleagues, in Harness-IF, test single rules against a withheld baseline, but on tasks written for the benchmark. And the registered report by Voria and colleagues, with Dr. Kashiwa, plans to relate file changes to code quality. As far as I know, no study does these three things together.

Slide 5. Three research questions (about 40 seconds (85 words))

RQ1 is the core: remove one real rule and see whether agents follow it less often on the same tasks. RQ2 asks which kinds of rules work. I can test wording directly, because I reword the same rule; specificity and linter coverage differ between rules, so those are associations. RQ3 asks whether keeping a rule changes code quality. I compare file versions on the same task, not runs that happened to follow the rule, and I leave out any check that encodes the rule itself.

Slide 6. Design: one rule at a time, on real tasks (about 60 seconds (135 words))

A task is a merged pull request whose own tests fail before and pass after. The agent starts just before it, with no git history, and the task does not mention the rule. Every task runs with all five versions, so each task is its own control. The neutral sentence has the same length but no instruction, so comparing it with the original separates the rule's content from just having more text. A script measures what fraction of applicable places follow the rule, and I check each script by hand on at least 20 examples. Thirty rules, two tasks each, give at most 1,800 runs, about 1,300 to 1,900 dollars; a pilot sets the final numbers. Two limits: only rules a script can check, and one rule at a time cannot show how rules interact.

Slide 7. Two-year plan and expected results (about 45 seconds (101 words))

Year 1: courses in software engineering and statistics, the checkers and harness, the pilot, then the main experiment. I also start a study of real pull requests, which extends the indentation check in Agent READMEs to more rules, with human pull requests as a comparison. Year 2: code quality, a first paper, and a small checker that developers rate. Your pull request study recommends a guideline file like CLAUDE.md for project conventions. My question is whether agents then follow those rules, which is why I want to do this research here. Thank you. I would be glad to hear your advice.

Timing check: about 714 spoken words, which is just under 5 minutes 30 seconds at a calm pace (the slide times above add up to 5:25). If a rehearsal runs over 5:30, cut the Yuki sentence on slide 2 first.

3. The questions most likely to come after the slides

The reviewers who read the deck as Dr. Reid and Dr. Ji listed these. Answer short first, then stop. Longer answers are in 03_Research_Plan_Defense/05_question_bank_with_model_answers.md (IDs in brackets).

Q1. (Dr. Reid) Our Agent READMEs paper already checked an indentation rule before and after it was added. What does your study add? (C49)

Your check showed fewer violations after the rule was added, in two repositories, and the paper says two cases cannot establish causality. I want to test it in a controlled way: the same task and the same code, where only the file changes, for about 30 rules and two agents, and also look at code quality.

Q2. Gloaguen et al. report from agent traces that instructions are well followed. Why is RQ1 still open? (C40)

They compare whole files: no file, a file written by a language model, and the developer's file. Their evidence that instructions are followed comes from tool calls in the traces. For example, uv was used 1.6 times per task when the file mentioned it and almost never when it did not. That is about tool use, and it compares runs with different files. They do not remove or reword one rule in the same file on the same task, and they do not check rules in the code. Also, followed is not the same as effective, and effective is what I measure.

Q3. Harness-IF already tests single rules against runs with the rule withheld. What is new? (C42)

Harness-IF's rules started from a survey of real files, but they were rewritten into a library and placed into tasks the authors wrote, and most verdicts use a language model judge. I keep each rule inside its own repository's real file, run that repository's own merged pull requests, check compliance with scripts, and also measure code quality.

Q4. How is this different from Agent Skill Evolution [11]? (C43)

They studied Skill files, and only rules that name a command, path or identifier. Adding such a rule made agents take the required action more often, mainly when that command or path was new to the Skill. When the old Skill already named it, they found no clear gain in the agent runs. So they do not compare specific rules with general ones, which is one thing my RQ2 asks. Their requests were also written by a model. I test rules in real CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md files on real pull request tasks.

Q5. (Dr. Ji) What is your treatment, your control, and what could confound it? (C24)

The treatment is the file version. For RQ1 I compare the original with the rule removed, on the same task, so task difficulty is the same in both. The neutral sentence has the same length but no instruction, so original vs neutral tests the rule's content, and neutral vs removed tests just having more text. Wording is manipulated, so it is close to causal. Specificity and linter coverage differ between rules, so those are associations.

Q6. (Dr. Ji) You remove one rule at a time. What if rules interact? (C27)

One rule at a time cannot show interactions, and they are real: Zhang et al. tested five rule pairs on pass rate, and two were clearly not additive. Your CAM paper also shows features that matter mainly together with others. I measure each rule with the rest of the real file in place, which is what a developer faces when deleting a rule, so I describe each result as the effect of removing that one rule from that real file. If the pilot budget allows, I could test a few related pairs and compare them with the sum of the single effects.

Q7. (Dr. Ji) Compliance is a fraction. Why logistic regression? Are 3 runs enough? You test about 30 rules. (C22, C25, C26)

Compliance is a count: places that follow the rule out of the places where it applies, so a logistic model for counts fits. For RQ2 the rule property interacts with the file version, because effective means followed more when the rule is in the file than when it is removed. For complexity I would use a linear mixed model, and for warning counts a count model, with the same fixed and random effects. Three runs is few for one rule, so the main test pools all rules, with task and rule as random effects. For single rules I would report the size of the change with an interval and correct for testing many rules. The pilot shows the run-to-run spread and sets the final number of runs. At VTU, probability and basic statistical inference were part of my third-semester mathematics course, Mathematics for Computer Science. It covered probability distributions, sampling, hypothesis tests such as the t-test and chi-square test, and basic ANOVA. I have not taken a full statistics course. For this plan I studied logistic regression and mixed effects models on my own. A proper statistics course is in my plan for the first half of Year 1.

Q8. (Dr. Reid) How do you know your rule checkers are correct? What share of real rules can a script check? (C19, C12)

I check each script by hand on at least 20 examples and report its accuracy. Only rules a script can check are included, so my results speak for that kind of rule, not for design or process rules. I do not know the share yet; counting it is one of the first steps of the pilot.

Q9. (Dr. Reid) How do you build a task, and are there enough pull requests with tests that fail before and pass after? (C14)

I replay merged pull requests whose own tests fail before and pass after, with the context file as it was at that commit. The task text does not mention the rule. I do not know yet how many usable pull requests exist, so the pilot counts that first, and I prefer ones merged after the models' training cutoff.

Q10. If all tests are already in tests/, the agent copies that anyway. What if most rules show no effect? (C10, C37)

That is a real possibility. The no-file and rule-removed versions show how much the agent learns from the code itself. If removing a rule does not change compliance, I report an interval, so it is clear how big an effect I could have missed. With only a few tasks per rule, I would not call one rule useless. But if this happens for many rules, it suggests agents often follow the existing code anyway, and the no-file version shows that directly.

Q11. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md and Codex reads AGENTS.md. Is the agent effect mixed up with the file? (C17)

Both get exactly the same text; only the file name differs, because that is how each tool reads it. So "agent" means the tool and its model together. I do not claim to separate the model from the tool.

Q12. Public pull requests may be in the training data. (C16)

I prefer pull requests merged after the models' training cutoff, and I report older tasks separately, as Gloaguen et al. did with their cutoff split. Every file version runs on the same task, so mostly memorisation would pull all versions toward the merged code and make differences smaller. But the original file might cue that memory more than the edited versions, so I cannot fully rule out a false gap. The before and after cutoff comparison is how I check that.

Q13. Who pays the 1,300 to 1,900 US dollars? (C28)

It is a first estimate from the per-task costs in Gloaguen et al., and the pilot sets the real budget. I do not know yet who would pay. I would ask whether it fits a lab budget; otherwise I can reduce runs, or use an open-weight agent for part of the study. The pilot is different: I can pay for the two-repository pilot myself; it is a few hundred US dollars, about 265 to 375 dollars for 360 runs.

Note: never say the lab will pay.

Only if asked about the 20%: over 20% is their headline figure; for developer-written files, which I use, they report a cost increase of at most 19%.

Q14. (Dr. Reid) In the real pull request study, how do you find agent pull requests, and what about rules added right after violations? (C34, C35)

AIDev labels pull requests by agent. Rules are often added right after violations, so violations would drop anyway, and agents also improve over time. That is why I compare with human pull requests in the same repositories and report it as associations only.

Q15. (Dr. Reid) How will you evaluate the checker with developers? (C55)

A small study: a few developers look at each warning and say whether it is correct and useful. I know this is your area, and I would be glad of your advice on how to design it well.

Q16. In BrandMemory, what were the two arms of your A/B test? (B10)

The same product demo, generated without the rules and with the rules, after both fixes. I counted contractions and "you" and "your" in the output. Both demos were made in the same workspace, from the same source video, with the same request, "Announce a new feature to customers". In the text of both demos, contractions went from 6 to 0, and "you" and "your" from 15 to 1, which matches the rules "avoid contractions" and "write in the third person". I do not remember the exact word count of the demo text. It is one comparison, which is why I want to study this properly.

Q17. (Dr. Reid) Isn't this just the future work of our Manifests paper? (C48)

I read that section, and I was glad to see it. I came to this question from my own work, where some rules had no effect. My plan is narrower: I test single real rules, one at a time, on real tasks from the same repositories, and I measure with scripts both whether agents follow each rule and how the code quality changes.

Q18. (Dr. Ji) Compliance is a share of applicable places. What if a file version changes whether there is any applicable place? (C18)

I pair each rule with tasks where it applies, but it can still happen. For example, a test location rule might make the agent write tests at all. So for each version I report how many runs have an applicable place, as a result of its own. Runs with none are reported separately, not counted as followed or not followed. If removing a rule changes whether the agent writes tests, that is also an effect, and I report it.

Q19. How do you reword a rule without changing its meaning? (C11)

A fixed template flips only the polarity. For example, "put new tests in the tests folder" becomes "do not put new tests outside the tests folder". A second person checks every pair for the same meaning, and I report how often we agreed. If a rule cannot be flipped without adding or losing information, I do not reword it, and I report how many rules could be reworded. So the wording result is about this kind of rewording, not every possible phrasing.

Q20. Tell us more about Yuki. (B15)

Yuki is my personal AI agent for the desktop. I built it twice. Yuki for Mac is open source. It reads the accessibility tree, not screenshots, and runs on cloud or small local models. On my small eval set, with tool retrieval, a local 7B model picked the right first tool in 9 of 10 tasks. Fine-tuning helped a weak 1B model but hurt a stronger 3B model. Yuki 2.0 is a Windows rewrite. You talk to it, it works in your apps, and it keeps an encrypted memory on your PC. Before anything that sends, closes or deletes, a separate model checks the step against only your words. My main lesson: adding rule after rule made the agent rigid.

Key point: The Mac agent core is built on a fork of MacOS-Use, so say so if asked. If they ask what you built yourself, say:

Yuki for Mac is built on a fork of MacOS-Use, an MIT-licensed agent for macOS, and about half of its Python code is that vendored core. On top of it I built the Mac app itself, a SwiftUI menu bar app with a typed command bar that runs a Python backend, and I changed how the agent acts, so it presses the real accessibility element instead of clicking coordinates. For small local models I added tool retrieval, a leaner accessibility tree, a small eval set and LoRA fine-tuning experiments, and for control I added a hard stop after three identical actions in a row, a Stop button and an automatic pause when the user touches the mouse or keyboard. I also added a local memory of apps, window titles and music, and I shipped it from v0.1.0 to v0.5.1 through GitHub Releases and Homebrew.

Yuki 2.0 is my own rewrite for Windows, started from scratch on 22 September 2026, without the fork or any agent framework. I designed it around rules that live in code, not in the prompt: it reads Windows UI Automation instead of screenshots, every action is classed by whether it can be undone, and a separate checker model sees only the user's own words before any lasting step. I built the voice pipeline, the encrypted local memory with a secret filter, and the offline replays I use to test it; for example, the checker held 9 of 9 unasked actions with 0 of 36 false holds. I used coding agents such as Claude Code as tools for parts of the work, and I made the design decisions and reviewed and tested the changes.

Q21. Your proposal mentions Burnt. What is it? (B14)

Burnt is a small menu bar app for Mac and Windows. It runs the open source ccusage tool on Claude Code and Codex logs to show what they cost. It is a small utility, so the AI project I would rather tell you about is Yuki, my desktop agent. (Then give the Q20 answer.)
